title: Variational Quantum Circuit-Based Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Portfolio Optimization
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a Quantum Reinforcement Learning framework for dynamic portfolio optimization using Variational Quantum Circuits, implementing quantum analogues of DDPG and DQN. Empirical evaluation on real financial data shows quantum agents can match or exceed classical deep RL risk-adjusted performance while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters, though practical deployment is currently hampered by cloud-based QPU latency; the authors release their code as open source.
methodology_description: The study develops a fully quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) framework for dynamic portfolio optimization by implementing quantum analogues of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Deep Q-Network (DQN) using variational/parameterized quantum circuits (VQCs) as actor and critic function approximators. Classical financial observations are mapped to quantum states via an extended amplitude-encoding feature map Z(˜x) = [˜x, ˜x⊙2, sin(˜x), cos(˜x)] with normalization; this encoded state is processed by a PQC consisting of alternating parameterized single-qubit rotations and entangling layers. Actor outputs are obtained by measuring Pauli-Z expectation values on the first N qubits to produce marginal probabilities that are ℓ1-normalized to portfolio weights. Training is performed on a noiseless statevector simulator using exact gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule and standard classical optimizers (Adam), while inference (deployment) of the optimized circuits is evaluated on IBM superconducting hardware (Eagle r3). The RL training loop mirrors classical off-policy Actor-Critic designs: experience replay, target networks with soft updates (τ = 0.005), minibatch updates, critic MSE loss, deterministic policy-gradient updates for the actor, and exploration via Gaussian action noise for continuous actions. Model selection uses expanding-window time-series cross-validation (7 folds) and Bayesian hyperparameter search with the Sharpe ratio on validation sets as acquisition objective. Performance is reported as out-of-sample Sharpe ratio (transaction costs 0.15% applied), and comparisons are made against equal-weighted, mean-variance optimization (MVO), and classical DDPG/DQN baselines across multiple classical model sizes.
algorithms_used: Quantum DQN (VQC critic + parameterized actor sampling)
experimental_setup: Training: hybrid pipeline with all training on a noiseless statevector simulator executed on a GPU (Nvidia RTX 8000). Inference/Deployment: optimized VQCs executed on IBM Eagle r3 superconducting QPU (127 qubits) via cloud; QPU runs used 10,000 shots per circuit evaluation. Practical cloud access incurred multi-tenant queuing and per-forward-pass latency (~12s), leading to total job durations (examples) of ~23–43 minutes despite intrinsic circuit execution times being millisecond-scale.
dataset_used: Historical daily closing prices for 15 financial assets (mix of equities, ETFs, bonds and commodities) spanning August 2011 to September 2025 (5049 trading days). Returns computed as log differences. State representation uses a 30-day lookback window concatenated with a 7-day Auto ARIMA forecast for each asset. Full asset list provided in appendix (AAPL, EFA, GLD, IWM, JNJ, JPM, LQD, MSFT, QQQ, SPY, TLT, USO, XLF, XLV, XOM).

experiment_input.preprocessing: Log returns computed from closing prices; for each decision timestep the state is a concatenation of a 30-day normalized price window and a 7-day Auto ARIMA forecast. Inputs are normalized and transformed by feature map Z(˜x) = [˜x, ˜x⊙2, sin(˜x), cos(˜x)] before amplitude encoding. Transaction costs of 0.15% per trade applied to returns. overview_steps: Construct state: 30-day lookback + 7-day Auto ARIMA forecast per asset
Form normalized input ˜x and build extended feature map Z(˜x) = [˜x, ˜x⊙2, sin(˜x), cos(˜x)]
Amplitude-encode Z(˜x) into n-qubit quantum state (statevector simulator during training)
Apply parameterized VQC (alternating rotation layers + entangling gates) as actor and as critic
Readout: measure Pauli-Z on first N qubits to get expectation values; ℓ1-normalize to obtain portfolio weights (actor) or produce scalar critic estimate
Compute RL targets: for DDPG use target actor µ' and target critic Q'; for continuous DQN sample M candidate next actions and take max Q'
Update critic by minimizing MSE between Q and targets
Update actor via deterministic policy gradient using ∇a Q * ∇θµ µ(s)
Use parameter-shift rule to compute exact gradients for circuit parameters; optimizer = Adam (or SGD in tuning)
Use experience replay (unlimited buffer) and soft target updates τ = 0.005
Hyperparameter tuning by Bayesian search using validation Sharpe ratio; early stopping with patience 10 over up to 50 epochs
Deploy trained circuit to IBM Eagle r3 QPU for inference with 10,000 shots to evaluate real-hardware performance and latency.

reproducibility_notes: Authors provide an open-source code repository: https://github.com/VincentGurgul/qrl-dpo-public. Training used a noiseless statevector simulator (exact gradients via parameter-shift rule) and IBM Eagle r3 was used only for inference runs; hyperparameter search ranges and fixed hyperparameters (lookback 30d, forecast 7d, shots=10000, τ=0.005, epochs=50, early stopping=10, DQN next-action samples=10, replay buffer unlimited) are listed in the appendix. The precise market data vendor/source is not specified in the text but the full asset list and dates are given; reproducing identical results may therefore require access to the same historical price series or a stated equivalent. Hyperparameter search used Bayesian optimization with validation Sharpe as acquisition objective. The repository and appended hyperparameter ranges support reproducibility, although QPU inference requires IBM cloud access and may be subject to queueing/availability differences.

[supported] In empirical tests on a 15-asset, real-world dataset (5049 daily prices, Aug 2011–Sep 2025) with 30-day rebalancing, QRL agents with very few trainable parameters (30 and 60 parameters) achieved risk-adjusted performance (Sharpe ratios) comparable to many classical deep RL baselines while using several orders of magnitude fewer parameters.

results_summary: The preprint presents a fully quantum/hybrid QRL pipeline applying VQCs as actor and critic in continuous-action dynamic portfolio optimization on real financial data. Trained on a statevector simulator and deployed (inference-only) on IBM hardware, compact quantum agents (30–60 trainable parameters) achieved Sharpe ratios competitive with many classical deep RL baselines while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters. However, practical deployment was limited by cloud QPU overheads (queuing, initialization) that inflated end-to-end inference times to tens of minutes despite fast intrinsic circuit execution. The authors conclude QRL is empirically competitive in a low-parameter regime and potentially practically advantageous in the future as infrastructure and access models improve.

quantum_advantage_detail: The authors empirically show that compact VQC-based QRL agents can match or exceed some classical baselines' Sharpe ratios while using far fewer parameters in their experiments, but they do not demonstrate a general, reproducible quantum advantage over state-of-the-art classical methods. They characterize potential practical advantage as contingent on reduced cloud/hardware overheads and improved dedicated QPU access, making the claim forward-looking/speculative rather than demonstrated.
limitations: Training was performed on a noiseless statevector simulator while only inference was executed on a QPU, so training did not account for realistic hardware noise and finite-shot sampling.

Statevector simulation scales exponentially and constrained circuit width (~20 qubits) and model size (max ~60 trainable parameters in experiments), limiting the size of quantum models that could be trained.

End-to-end quantum inference on cloud-accessible QPUs is dominated by infrastructure overhead (queueing, repeated initialization, multi-tenant synchronization), producing minutes-scale runtimes despite millisecond native circuit execution.

Practical cloud QPU access is costly and low-throughput, making full training or large-scale hyperparameter searches on hardware prohibitively expensive (authors cite per-call latencies and monetary costs).

Current quantum hardware limitations—noise, limited qubit connectivity, and embedding constraints—reduce practical performance and challenge realization of a quantum advantage (stated in literature review).
Variational circuits suffer from barren plateaus (vanishing gradients) as system size and depth increase, constraining circuit depth and trainability.
Amplitude (state-preparation) encoding can require O(2^n) gates for an n-qubit register (state-preparation overhead), which may be expensive or impractical on near-term hardware.
The parameter-shift gradient estimation method requires two circuit evaluations per trainable parameter, increasing quantum evaluation overhead on hardware.

How will realistic hardware noise, finite-shot measurement noise, and limited qubit connectivity affect training dynamics, convergence, and out-of-sample performance when training is performed on-device rather than on a noiseless simulator?
What circuit ansatzes, initialization schemes, and encoding strategies best mitigate barren plateaus while preserving expressivity for financial time-series tasks?
How does QRL scale with larger asset universes, longer lookback/forecast windows, and more complex state representations—can the observed parameter efficiency be maintained at scale?
Does the parameter-efficiency of VQCs translate into improved sample efficiency, robustness, and generalization across different market regimes compared to classical counterparts?
What are the trade-offs between different data-encoding schemes (angle, amplitude, feature maps) in terms of state-preparation cost, expressivity, and hardware requirements for portfolio problems?

Is full end-to-end training (including gradient estimation) on cloud QPUs economically and technically feasible in the near future, or will hybrid training/simulator approaches remain necessary for the foreseeable term?
How does the economic cost-benefit compare between deploying QRL (including QPU access costs and infrastructure) versus scaled classical Deep RL on modern classical hardware?
How sensitive are the reported results to choices such as forecast model (Auto ARIMA), rebalancing frequency, transaction cost assumptions, and other environment design decisions?
